correctness.rationale: Conditioning on the hub gives the stated degree-(m+1) polynomial. The equality |1+2z|=|1+z| on the stated circle and the strict bound |z|≤2/3 give exactly m interior zeros by Rouché, with none on the boundary. On the negative real axis write z=−x. For 0<x<1/2 the positive ratio (1−2x)/(1−x) decreases from 1 to 0; its m-th power thus crosses x once. For 1/2<x<1 both terms have the same negative sign when m is odd, whereas for even m the log derivative of ((2x−1)/(1−x))^m/x is 2m/(2x−1)+m/(1−x)−1/x>0, and the ratio already exceeds 1 at 2/3. For x>1 the ratio equation becomes x=(2+1/(x−1))^m with a strictly decreasing right-hand side bounded below by 2^m. This proves uniqueness of the exterior zero and the real census, including m=1,2. Differentiation at any multiple zero gives mz=(1+2z)(1+z); for m≥3 its candidates have nonnegative real part, excluded by the root locations, and for m=1,2 all roots are already distinct by the count. Writing Q=2^m, the exterior equation first gives X_m−Q=O(m) by exponentiation and then gives X_m−Q=mQ/[2(X_m−1)]+O(m²/Q)=m/2+O(m²/Q). Under w=(1+2z)/(1+z), an interior zero satisfies |w|^m=|w−1|/|2−w|. On |w|≤1−ε the left side tends uniformly to zero and the right side is at least ε/3; the inverse Möbius map transfers the uniform boundary approach. This is not a claim of angular equidistribution. The accompanying graph/Sturm checks were inspected, not run, and do not certify the complex all-m assertions.

evidence: Zhang–Tu's strict left-half-plane theorem applies to all spiders.

Sokal's general limiting-zero theorem classifies subsequential finite limiting zeros via a zero of a uniquely dominant amplitude or a tie of dominant bases. Here the bases are 1+2z and 1+z, nondegenerate, with amplitudes 1 and z. The only amplitude zero is on the equimodular circle. Thus the limit set in the finite plane is the circle, which together with compactness of the interior zeros implies uniform radial approach.
